title: The Beatitudes as the summit
hookLine: blessed are: the portrait of Christ and of a saint
tomorrow: saints are for other people. or are they?

lines: DESCRIBE YOURSELF IN A FEW WORDS.
cards: Every profile asks for it: describe yourself in a few words. The usual answers are wins. Driven.
Funny. Loves travel. Now read a different kind of bio.
Hungry for justice. Merciful. Clean of heart.

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.
teach.b: The question is old: what does a holy life look like? Catholics answer with this list. It opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."
The Catechism says the Beatitudes depict the face of Jesus Christ himself. Meek, merciful, a peacemaker, persecuted: that's his life, line by line.

And because saints are people who come to look like him, it's their portrait too. That's why the path calls it the summit: five years of saints and stories, and this is the face they share. Now the neighbor.
One line, "Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the land," has an older sister.

teach.h: THE HUMBLE SHALL INHERIT THE LAND.
teach.b: Psalm thirty-seven, in the Jewish Publication Society's translation: "But the humble shall inherit the land, and delight themselves in the abundance of peace."
The psalms are still prayed in Jewish prayer, and the Hebrew word for happy, ashrei, opens the very first psalm. Jesus, a Jew, speaking on a hillside, is singing a line his listeners already knew.
That's shared ground: the humble are the ones who inherit.
And the honest difference: for Catholics, the Beatitudes are finally a portrait of Jesus. Jewish readers hear Psalm thirty-seven as God's promise to the humble, without that portrait.
Same words, held in two different hands, and neither has to be ranked.

how: Catholics hear the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12) at Mass, notably on All Saints' Day, and some use them as an examination of conscience.

games.q: what does “the beatitudes as the summit” mean?
o: the blessed are lines, read as one face: Christ's
the Ten Commandments in a newer, gentler form
a list of rewards saved for the end of time

games.q: one portrait, two voices — tap the pairs.
p: theirs is the kingdom of heaven
the humble shall inherit the land

s: the Beatitudes are rules you must keep to get into heaven
the Catechism calls them a portrait: the face of Jesus Christ, and of those who grow like him.
blessed are the meek echoes a line from the Psalms
Psalm 37: the humble shall inherit the land.
Jews and Catholics read Psalm 37 the same way
they share the words; Catholics also see Jesus's portrait in them, and Jewish readers hear God's promise to the humble.

games.q: your Jewish teammate hears "blessed are the meek" and says, "that's from a psalm i know." what's the fair reply?
o: "no, Jesus said it first; that's the Gospel."
"yes, it echoes Psalm 37. we read it a bit differently."
"so it's all the same thing, really."
games.why: Matthew's line echoes Psalm 37:11. the words are shared ground; for Catholics they also become a portrait of Jesus. shared, and honestly different.

practice: Take a pen and write one beatitude by hand, the one that feels furthest from you today: meek, merciful, peacemaker, clean of heart. Write it slowly, then look at it while the sit runs.
If you pray, you can ask for that one line to show up in your face today.

wordCard.voice: The Beatitudes as the summit. The blessed are lines: a portrait of Christ, and of everyone who comes to look like him.

orig.note: Greek: blessed, happy. the first word of each Beatitude in Matthew 5.

carryVoice: The line to keep: the portrait, every line a brushstroke of one face, with room in it for yours. Talk tomorrow.
